passage: Week one: Ayesha, sixteen, scrolled short videos in bed until two every night, then dragged herself to school with a headache. Her sister Preeti found her asleep over her books on Thursday. Week two: Ayesha tried a rule: phone charging in the kitchen after ten. The first night she lay awake, itchy, reaching for a phone that wasn't there. The third night she read a novel instead and fell asleep by eleven. Week four: her headaches had eased, and she'd finished two chapters of revision before breakfast. "I still miss it," she admitted to Preeti. "But I don't miss feeling like a zombie."

qa.q: Where did Ayesha charge her phone after ten?
qa.a: In the kitchen.

qa.q: What was Ayesha feeling the first night without her phone?
qa.a: She felt restless and uncomfortable, missing the habit badly.

qa.q: What made Ayesha's new rule work?
qa.a: It was simple and physical, keeping the phone out of reach, and she replaced scrolling with reading.

qa.q: How might Preeti see the change in her sister?
qa.a: Relieved and impressed that Ayesha stuck with it despite the struggle.

grounding: Shows a teenager moving from late-night screen use to a healthier routine over a month.

passage: "Hansa, you asked why I never smoked. When I, your Jatin Mama, was sixteen, the boys behind the bus depot all did, and gutka too. One evening they held out a packet to me. 'Just try, don't be a baby.' My hands were in my pockets, sweaty. I knew what it had done to my uncle's teeth and lungs. I said, 'I have football at six,' and walked away. They laughed. So I made football my excuse every day, and then it stopped being an excuse. I ran every morning for ten years. Those boys still call me 'Coach'."

qa.q: What excuse did young Jatin give when offered the packet?
qa.a: "I have football at six."

qa.q: What was young Jatin feeling with his sweaty hands in his pockets?
qa.a: He felt pressured and nervous, afraid of being mocked but determined not to start.

qa.q: What turning point in the story built Jatin's lasting habit?
qa.a: Using football as his excuse every day until it became a real routine.

qa.q: How might the boys behind the depot have seen Jatin later?
qa.a: With some respect, since they now call him "Coach".

grounding: Shows an elder recalling how as a teenager he resisted substance pressure and built a healthy habit instead.

passage: Board exams were six weeks away, and Bhupen, seventeen, was playing online games until three every night. His marks were sliding. His mother Farida didn't want a fight, so one evening she sat beside him. "How many hours today?" He shrugged. "Five? Six?" "And studying?" "One." She didn't take the phone. "Make me a plan you can actually keep." He grumbled, then wrote: two hours of games on weekends only, phone out of the room at eleven, study in forty-minute blocks. The first week he broke it twice. The second week, once. Farida noticed and said nothing, just left a plate of cut fruit by his desk.

qa.q: How many weeks away were the board exams?
qa.a: Six weeks away.

qa.q: What might Bhupen have been feeling when he admitted to five or six hours?
qa.a: Probably guilty and a bit embarrassed, knowing his marks were sliding.

qa.q: Why did Farida's approach work better than taking the phone?
qa.a: Letting Bhupen make the plan gave him ownership, so he was more likely to stick to it.

qa.q: How might Farida feel in the second week?
qa.a: Quietly relieved and hopeful as he breaks the plan less often.

grounding: Shows a teenager, with his mother's help, working to control heavy gaming under exam time pressure.

passage: I'm Damini, from the flat across the corridor. Chandrika, who's seventeen, stopped her cousin at the gate last Sunday. He was about to ride off on the scooter without a helmet. "It's the law, and you know Papa's rule: nobody from our house gets a challan," she said, holding out the helmet. He rolled his eyes but wore it. She also volunteers with the colony's traffic awareness drive and reads the rules out loud to anyone who'll listen. I can't tell if it's pride or worry, but she clearly cares what her family's name stands for.

qa.q: What did Chandrika hold out to her cousin?
qa.a: The helmet.

qa.q: What might Chandrika have felt when her cousin rolled his eyes?
qa.a: Probably a little annoyed, but firm and protective, caring more about his safety than his mood.

qa.q: What would you advise Chandrika to keep her message from sounding preachy?
qa.a: Explain the reasons calmly and set an example, rather than lecturing everyone she meets.

qa.q: How does Damini see Chandrika's actions?
qa.a: Damini notices real care for the law and family name, though unsure whether it's pride or worry.

grounding: Shows a teenager respecting traffic law and her family's standards, seen by a neighbour.

passage: Monday: Asif, sixteen, found a phone on the bus seat, locked, battery low. His friend said, "Keep it." Asif took it home. Tuesday: his uncle Tanvir said, "You don't keep what isn't yours. Take it to the police station." Asif was nervous; he'd never been inside one. Wednesday: the constable at the desk wrote down his name, logged the phone and thanked him. "Most people don't bother." A week later, the owner, an old schoolteacher, called to thank him. Asif told Tanvir, "I thought police stations were scary. They were just… doing their job."

qa.q: Who was the phone's owner?
qa.a: An old schoolteacher.

qa.q: What was Asif feeling about going to the police station?
qa.a: He felt nervous, never having been inside one before.

qa.q: What did Tanvir do that helped Asif act rightly?
qa.a: He made clear that keeping it was wrong and pointed to the proper place to hand it in.

qa.q: How might the constable see Asif handing in the phone?
qa.a: With appreciation, since most people don't bother.

grounding: Shows a teenager learning to trust public institutions by doing his civic duty with a lost phone.

passage: "Devika, you think voting is a small thing? When I, your Disha Nani, was seventeen, too young to vote, my father was a polling officer in our village. He took me along to carry the ink and the forms. I watched an old woman walk three kilometres, barefoot, to put her mark on a paper. My father treated her like the most important person in the room. Afterwards he said, 'Our family's honour is not our land. It's doing this job properly.' The next year, on my first vote, I wore my best sari."

qa.q: What did young Disha carry to the polling booth?
qa.a: The ink and the forms.

qa.q: What was young Disha feeling as she watched the old woman vote?
qa.a: She felt moved and full of admiration for the woman's effort and her father's respect.

qa.q: What turning point in the story shaped Disha's sense of civic duty?
qa.a: Seeing her father treat the old woman with respect and hearing what family honour meant to him.

qa.q: How might the old woman have felt being treated so respectfully?
qa.a: Valued and proud that her vote mattered.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling how as a teenager she learned civic duty and a sense of family honour at a polling booth.

passage: Monday: a private photo of Gargi, taken at a sleepover, appeared in Seema's class group with a mocking caption. Seema, fifteen, felt sick. Tuesday: people kept forwarding it. A friend told Seema, "Just laugh, everyone is." She didn't forward it. She reported it in the app, messaged Gargi, "I'm with you. Want to tell Ma'am together?" and they went to the class teacher that afternoon. The teacher had it removed and spoke to the class. Wednesday: Seema also finished her maths assignment on time, even with everything going on, and slept early. Gargi sat with her at lunch.

qa.q: Where did the private photo appear?
qa.a: In Seema's class group.

qa.q: What was Seema feeling when she first saw the photo?
qa.a: She felt sick and upset, knowing it was cruel to Gargi.

qa.q: What did Seema do right in handling it?
qa.a: She refused to forward it, reported it, supported Gargi and went to the teacher the same afternoon.

qa.q: How might Gargi feel when Seema messages her?
qa.a: Less alone and grateful to have someone on her side.

grounding: Shows a teenager rejecting online bullying, practising cyber ethics and still keeping up with her duties.

passage: "Saurabh, I'll tell you about the exam paper. When I, your Chetan Chacha, was sixteen, someone got the maths question paper the night before, and a photo went round our group. My friend said, 'Everyone's seen it. You'll be the only fool.' I sat with my phone for an hour, thumb over the image. I didn't open it. The next morning I told the principal, even though I knew people would hate me. The exam was cancelled and redone. Some boys didn't speak to me for months. But my name stayed clean, and that mattered more to me than marks."

qa.q: What went round young Chetan's group?
qa.a: A photo of the maths question paper.

qa.q: What was young Chetan feeling with his thumb over the image?
qa.a: He felt tempted and afraid of being the only one without it, but uneasy about cheating.

qa.q: What turning point in the story protected Chetan's reputation?
qa.a: Choosing not to open the photo and telling the principal the next morning.

qa.q: How might the boys who stopped speaking to Chetan have felt?
qa.a: Angry and resentful at having the exam redone, even though they had cheated.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling how as a teenager he protected his reputation and practised digital ethics about a leaked paper.

passage: It was the night before the chemistry exam, and Sumit, seventeen, was also looking after his grandmother, who had a fever, because his parents were at a wedding. At ten, his friend Bhupen messaged: "Got the answers from a guy who knows someone. Want?" Sumit looked at his notes, then at his grandmother dozing on the sofa. He typed, "No thanks. And don't forward it." He checked her water, warmed the soup his mother had left out, and studied at the dining table until midnight, getting up every half hour to check on her. He went to bed tired but with a clear head.

qa.q: Who was Sumit looking after?
qa.a: His grandmother, who had a fever.

qa.q: What might Sumit have felt when Bhupen's message came?
qa.a: He probably felt tempted and stressed, but also uneasy about cheating.

qa.q: What made Sumit's night a responsible one?
qa.a: He refused the answers, cared for his grandmother as his mother had arranged, and studied honestly.

qa.q: How might Bhupen see Sumit's reply?
qa.a: He might be annoyed or embarrassed, or it might make him rethink the answers too.

grounding: Shows a teenager balancing family duty, honest study and online ethics under time pressure.

passage: First month in Bengaluru: Vikas, nineteen, had his first stipend and no parents watching. By the twentieth, he was eating instant noodles and borrowing from his flatmate Devika. Second month: Devika showed him her notebook, every expense written down. Vikas started one too. He was shocked to see how much went on food deliveries. Third month: he paid the electricity bill the day it arrived, split the Wi-Fi fairly with Devika, and cooked rice and dal three nights a week. On the thirtieth, he still had money left, and he felt, for the first time, like an adult.

qa.q: What was Vikas eating by the twentieth of the first month?
qa.a: Instant noodles.

qa.q: How did Vikas feel on the thirtieth of the third month?
qa.a: He felt proud and grown-up, having managed the whole month on his own.

qa.q: What helped Vikas turn things around?
qa.a: Writing down every expense, as Devika did, so he could see where his money was going.

qa.q: How might Devika feel lending money in the first month?
qa.a: Maybe a little uneasy, but willing to help and share her own method.

grounding: Shows a young adult learning over three months to budget and pay bills without parental oversight.

passage: "Sudha, you're moving out next month, so listen. When I, your Gurpreet Bua, was twenty, I took a job in Mumbai and rented a tiny room. Nobody told me rent was due on the first, and the landlord knocked on the second. I was so ashamed. That night I sat with a school notebook and wrote down rent, electricity, bus pass, tiffin, everything. I was short. So I went to the bank near my office, and a kind officer there helped me open an account and set a reminder for rent. After that, I paid on the first, every month, for eight years."

qa.q: When was young Gurpreet's rent due?
qa.a: On the first.

qa.q: What was young Gurpreet feeling when the landlord knocked on the second?
qa.a: She felt ashamed and caught out, not knowing the rent was due.

qa.q: What turning point in the story helped Gurpreet manage her money?
qa.a: Writing down every expense and asking the bank officer for help that same week.

qa.q: How might the bank officer have seen young Gurpreet?
qa.a: As a nervous young worker who needed guidance, and was glad to help.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling how as a young adult she learned to manage rent and expenses alone, with help from a bank officer.

passage: The electricity bill was due tomorrow, and Indu, twenty-one, had just learned her salary would be late by a week. Her flatmate Anirban had already paid his share of the rent. Indu sat at the kitchen table with a notebook, listing what she had and what was due. The bill, groceries and the bus pass wouldn't all fit. She felt her chest tighten. Instead of panicking, she called the electricity office to ask about the late fee, then texted her landlord to explain. Anirban offered to cover groceries this week. "I'll pay you back on the fifth," she said, and wrote it down.

qa.q: How late would Indu's salary be?
qa.a: By a week.

qa.q: What was Indu feeling when she realised everything wouldn't fit?
qa.a: She felt anxious and tense, her chest tightening.

qa.q: What was sensible about how Indu handled it?
qa.a: She listed what was due, contacted the electricity office and landlord early, and wrote down what she owed Anirban.

qa.q: How might Anirban feel about covering groceries?
qa.a: Glad to help, and reassured that Indu is being clear about paying him back.

grounding: Shows a young adult managing bills and expenses under a delayed salary without parental help.

passage: In their student flat in Paris, Leila, nineteen, pulled her laundry out of the machine: every white shirt was now pale pink. A red sock lay at the bottom like evidence. Her flatmate Nour laughed so hard she had to sit down. "Welcome to adult life." Leila groaned. That evening Nour showed her how to sort colours, check labels and pick the right setting. On Sunday, Leila made her first proper lentil soup, cleaned the stove afterwards without being asked, and wrote a weekly chore chart for the fridge. The pink shirts stayed pink. She wore them anyway.

qa.q: What turned Leila's white shirts pink?
qa.a: A red sock.

qa.q: How did Leila feel when she saw the pink shirts?
qa.a: She felt frustrated and a bit embarrassed at her laundry mistake.

qa.q: What did Leila do well after the mistake?
qa.a: She learned from Nour, cooked and cleaned on her own, and set up a chore chart.

qa.q: How might Nour see Leila's progress?
qa.a: Amused at first, then pleased to see her flatmate learning to run the home.

grounding: Shows a young adult learning to handle laundry, cooking and cleaning independently.

passage: In the college hostel's shared kitchen, Keerthana, eighteen, stared at a pan of burnt rice. At home, Amma had always cooked. The warden, Payal Ma'am, came in, sniffed the air and smiled. "Too much heat, not enough water. Try again." Keerthana did, measuring this time. It came out sticky but edible. Over the next weeks she learned to wash her own clothes in a bucket, sweep her room every morning and fix the loose hook on her cupboard with a borrowed screwdriver. When she went home for Diwali, she made the dal herself. Amma watched and didn't say a word, just nodded.

qa.q: What had Keerthana burnt?
qa.a: A pan of rice.

qa.q: What was Keerthana feeling when she stared at the burnt rice?
qa.a: She felt frustrated and a little lost, never having cooked alone before.

qa.q: What helped Keerthana learn to manage on her own?
qa.a: Payal Ma'am's calm tip and her own willingness to keep trying week after week.

qa.q: How might Amma feel watching Keerthana make the dal?
qa.a: Proud and a bit moved to see her daughter so independent.

grounding: Shows a young adult learning to cook, clean and handle daily maintenance in a hostel.

passage:
Dear Binita Didi,
Three months in the flat now, and I have news: I can make dal that doesn't taste like water. Also, the kitchen tap started dripping last week. I watched a video, bought a washer from the hardware shop, and fixed it myself. I nearly flooded the floor first, but still. I do laundry every Sunday, sweep every other day, and I've learned that if you don't clean the stove right away, it's a nightmare later. Some nights I just eat bread and bananas, I won't lie. But I'm managing. You always said I couldn't boil an egg. I can now. Come and taste it.
Ganga

qa.q: What did Ganga buy from the hardware shop?
qa.a: A washer.

qa.q: How does Ganga seem to feel about managing the flat?
qa.a: Ganga feels proud and a bit cheeky, pleased to prove Didi wrong.

qa.q: What small habit is helping Ganga most?
qa.a: Cleaning the stove straight away and keeping a regular laundry and sweeping routine.

qa.q: How might Binita feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Amused and proud to see Ganga so independent.

grounding: Shows a young adult proudly handling cooking, cleaning and small repairs on their own.

passage: I'm Lavanya, Vishal's flatmate. In our first semester, Vishal, nineteen, slept till noon, skipped morning lectures, and started assignments at midnight. There was no bell, no parent, no one to make him. After failing a quiz, he came into the kitchen looking shaken. The next week he'd taped a timetable to the wall: lectures in green, library in blue, cricket in red, sleep at midnight. He set two alarms. He missed some blocks, but by the end of the month he was in class on time and cooking dinner at seven. I don't know what changed exactly, but that timetable is still up.

qa.q: What colour were the lectures on Vishal's timetable?
qa.a: Green.

qa.q: What might Vishal have felt after failing the quiz?
qa.a: He probably felt shaken and worried, realising his loose routine was costing him.

qa.q: What would you advise Vishal about the blocks he misses?
qa.a: Treat misses as normal, adjust the timetable if needed, and restart the next block instead of giving up.

qa.q: How does Lavanya see Vishal's change?
qa.a: Lavanya is impressed that he stuck with it, though unsure exactly what changed.

grounding: Shows a young adult learning to structure unstructured time without bells or parents, seen by a flatmate.

passage: First week of the second year: Shreya, twenty, had three-hour gaps between classes and spent them scrolling in the canteen. Her friend Anand noticed. "You could finish assignments in those gaps." Fourth week: she started using her phone's calendar, blocking each gap for reading, the gym or lunch with friends. Some days she ignored it. Exam week: while others were panicking, Shreya had her notes ready. She still pulled one late night, but only one. "The gaps were my time all along," she told Anand. "I just never used them."

qa.q: How long were the gaps between Shreya's classes?
qa.a: Three hours.

qa.q: How did Shreya feel during exam week compared with others?
qa.a: She felt calmer and more prepared while others were panicking.

qa.q: What helped Shreya use her time better?
qa.a: Blocking each gap in her calendar for a clear purpose, even if she didn't always follow it.

qa.q: How might Anand feel about Shreya's change?
qa.a: Pleased that his comment made a difference.

grounding: Shows a young adult learning to plan free time between classes over a term.

passage: "Baljeet, first year of college? Let me tell you. When I, your Simran Bua, was nineteen, I thought no bells meant freedom. I watched films till three and missed half my lectures. By November, I was behind in everything. My friend showed me her library timetable: same seat, same hours, every day, like a job. I copied it. At first I hated it. Then I noticed I had evenings free, really free, without guilt. By exams I was caught up. The trick wasn't working harder. It was deciding the time in advance."

qa.q: What did Simran's friend show her?
qa.a: Her library timetable.

qa.q: How did young Simran feel by November?
qa.a: She felt overwhelmed and behind, realising freedom had become chaos.

qa.q: What turning point in the story fixed Simran's schedule?
qa.a: Copying her friend's fixed library timetable and treating study like a job.

qa.q: How might Simran's friend have seen her struggles?
qa.a: With sympathy, wanting to help by sharing what worked for her.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling how as a young adult she learned to structure unstructured college time.

passage:
Dear Anand Mama,
I'm writing because I've decided something, and I want you to hear it from me. I'm leaving BCom after this year. I've spent two years in lectures I don't care about while spending every free hour in your workshop, sanding and joining wood. I've applied for the furniture design and carpentry course at the polytechnic. Papa is worried about money and status. I've made a plan: I'll work part-time at your workshop if you'll have me, and I'll show him the placement numbers. I'm scared. But when I'm making something, I feel like myself. Will you help me talk to him?
Ira

qa.q: Which course did Ira apply for?
qa.a: The furniture design and carpentry course at the polytechnic.

qa.q: How does Ira feel about the decision?
qa.a: Ira feels scared but sure, feeling most alive while making things.

qa.q: What makes Ira's plan more convincing?
qa.a: It has a concrete course, a part-time job idea and facts to show Papa, not just feelings.

qa.q: How might Anand Mama feel reading the letter?
qa.a: Touched and proud that Ira found a passion in his workshop, and a little worried about Papa.

grounding: Shows a young adult committing to a specialised trade path and planning how to pursue it.

passage: Thanks, Preeti, for having me on your campus radio show. I'm Asif, twenty-one, final-year agriculture. People ask why I chose farming science when I could've done engineering. Honestly, I tried engineering prep for a year and felt nothing. Then during lockdown I was back in my village, watching my father lose half his tomato crop to a pest. I spent nights reading about soil and pests. I realised I wanted to understand this, not escape it. So I switched. Now I'm specialising in soil health. It's harder than I thought. But every lab test feels like it matters for someone like my father.

qa.q: What is Asif specialising in?
qa.a: Soil health.

qa.q: What did Asif feel watching his father lose half the tomato crop?
qa.a: Asif felt upset and helpless, and then driven to understand the problem.

qa.q: What turning point in Asif's story led to the specialisation?
qa.a: The lockdown months in the village, seeing the crop loss and reading about soil and pests.

qa.q: How might Asif's father see the career choice?
qa.a: Probably with pride, knowing the father's own struggle shaped this path.

grounding: Shows a young adult committing to a specialised field after a personal turning point.

passage: I'm Pradeep, Hafsa's younger brother. For two years Hafsa, now twenty, drifted between courses: economics, then psychology, then back. Last summer she started volunteering with a local news website, writing about water shortages in our area. I'd never seen her so busy. She interviewed tanker drivers at six in the morning and wrote until midnight. In September she told our parents she was switching to journalism. There was an argument, but she had her articles printed out and ready. I don't know if she's sure, but she hasn't changed her mind since.

qa.q: What did Hafsa write about while volunteering?
qa.a: Water shortages in their area.

qa.q: What might Hafsa have felt while writing until midnight?
qa.a: She seemed energised and absorbed, finally caring deeply about her work.

qa.q: What would you advise Hafsa now that she has chosen journalism?
qa.a: Keep building a portfolio and find a mentor in the field to guide her next steps.

qa.q: How does Pradeep see his sister's change?
qa.a: He notices she's never been so busy and determined, though he can't be sure she's certain.

grounding: Shows a young adult moving from drifting to committing to a career path, seen by her brother.

passage: I'm Varun, and I've worked at this small accounting firm for three years. This summer Minakshi, twenty-one, joined as an intern straight from her BCom. In the first week she could barely use a spreadsheet beyond adding numbers. By the second week, she was staying back to watch me build formulas, writing each one in a notebook. By the end of the month she'd built a tracker for our client invoices that saved us an hour a day. I don't know how she learned so fast, but she never pretended to know something she didn't.

qa.q: What did Minakshi build by the end of the month?
qa.a: A tracker for client invoices.

qa.q: What might Minakshi have felt in the first week?
qa.a: She probably felt out of her depth and nervous, knowing so little about spreadsheets.

qa.q: What habit helped Minakshi learn quickly?
qa.a: Watching an experienced colleague and writing down each formula to practise.

qa.q: How does Varun see Minakshi's growth?
qa.a: Varun is impressed by how fast she learned and respects her honesty about what she didn't know.

grounding: Shows a young adult moving from general study to mastering a practical workplace skill, seen by a colleague.

passage: Week one of the welding course: Omkar, twenty, burned his forearm through his sleeve and his first joins looked like melted wax. The instructor, Gurleen, said, "Slower. Watch the pool, not the spark." Week five: his joins held, but they were uneven. He stayed after class every day to practise on scrap, ignoring his friends' calls to come for chai. Some evenings his joins still cracked, and he wanted to throw the torch down. He didn't. Week twelve: Gurleen tested his work with a hammer. It held. She handed him his certificate. "Now you have a skill someone will pay for." Omkar looked at his scarred hands and grinned.

qa.q: What did Gurleen use to test Omkar's work?
qa.a: A hammer.

qa.q: How did Omkar feel when Gurleen handed him the certificate?
qa.a: He felt proud and hopeful, knowing his hard work had given him a real skill.

qa.q: What helped Omkar master welding?
qa.a: Following Gurleen's advice and practising on scrap every day after class.

qa.q: How might Gurleen see Omkar's progress over the twelve weeks?
qa.a: With pride, seeing a student who kept going through burns and uneven joins.

grounding: Shows a young adult mastering a marketable trade skill over a course.

passage: "Kashish, you're worried you don't know enough for this job? When I, your Mahima Didi here at the office, was twenty-one, I joined the studio knowing nothing about video editing. I had a degree in English. My first cut was so bad the client laughed. That night I stayed and re-edited it scene by scene, watching how our senior editor did transitions. Every evening for six months, I practised on old footage. Slowly, my cuts got clean. By the next year, clients were asking for me. Skills aren't magic. They're a hundred bad drafts you don't give up on."

qa.q: What was young Mahima's degree in?
qa.a: English.

qa.q: What was young Mahima feeling when the client laughed?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and discouraged by her first poor edit.

qa.q: What turning point in the story began Mahima's mastery?
qa.a: Staying back that night to re-edit and then practising every evening for months.

qa.q: How might the senior editor have seen young Mahima?
qa.a: As a keen learner worth encouraging, since she kept studying his work.

grounding: Shows a senior colleague recalling how she moved from a general degree to mastering a professional skill.

passage: I'm Baljeet. In my second year, I went to a design workshop in Chandigarh and almost didn't speak to anyone. The main speaker was Jasleen, who ran a small studio I admired. At the tea break, my hands were shaking, but I walked up and said, "I liked how you explained colour. Could I show you my sketchbook?" She flipped through it, said, "Your layouts are strong, your lettering needs work," and gave me her email. I wrote to her the next day, thanking her. Two months later, she offered me a summer internship. I still email her when I'm stuck.

qa.q: What did Jasleen say needed work?
qa.a: The lettering.

qa.q: How did Baljeet feel walking up to Jasleen at the tea break?
qa.a: Baljeet felt nervous and shaky, but determined not to miss the chance.

qa.q: What small steps helped Baljeet build this connection?
qa.a: Speaking up at the break, showing real work and following up with a thank-you email the next day.

qa.q: How might Jasleen have seen Baljeet's approach?
qa.a: As brave and sincere, which made her willing to offer advice and later an internship.

grounding: Shows a young adult building a first professional connection that leads to a mentor and an internship.

passage:
Internship supervisor's note, Sharmila, June
Harish (20) has been with our NGO for four weeks. He asks good questions and writes down the answers. In week two he asked if he could sit in on the field team's meetings, and he now shadows our programme lead on Tuesdays. He's also reached out to two of our older volunteers for advice about careers in public health research. He's a little shy in large meetings, but one-to-one he's thoughtful. I've offered to write him a reference and introduced him to a researcher I know.

qa.q: How long has Harish been with the NGO?
qa.a: Four weeks.

qa.q: What might Harish feel in large meetings?
qa.a: He probably feels shy and a little anxious, though he's confident one-to-one.

qa.q: Why is Sharmila's introduction a helpful next step?
qa.a: It connects Harish with someone in the exact field he's interested in, building his network.

qa.q: How might the programme lead see Harish shadowing on Tuesdays?

"Vikas, look at this." Damini spread a row of cloth scraps on the table.
"Pink, yellow, brown… so?"
"Onion skins, turmeric, tea. From our kitchen bin."
"You dyed cloth with rubbish?"
"With biology." Damini, twenty-one, grinned. "Remember my microbiology class? Some bacteria fix colour better than salt does. And fashion is drowning in chemical dyes."
"So you're mixing lab stuff with clothes."
"And food waste. That's the idea. A dye kit for small tailors."
"Does it wash out?"
"The tea one does. The turmeric doesn't. I'm testing."
Vikas picked up the yellow scrap. "Can you make this blue?"
"Not yet," she said. "Give me a month."

passage: I'm Zeenat. In my last year of college, I was studying maths but spending evenings playing tabla. My friend Yamini, who studies computer science, laughed when I said rhythm was just fractions you can hear. "Prove it." So we did. We built a small app for children: tap a rhythm, and it shows you the fraction on screen, halves, quarters, triplets. Kids at the tuition centre loved it. They'd tap and giggle and suddenly understand quarters. It didn't come from maths or music alone. It came from sitting between them. Now, whenever I get stuck on a problem, I ask which other subject might already know the answer.

qa.q: What did the app show when children tapped a rhythm?
qa.a: The fraction on screen, halves, quarters, triplets.

qa.q: How did Zeenat feel seeing the children use the app?
qa.a: Zeenat felt delighted and proud watching them giggle and understand quarters.

qa.q: What made Zeenat and Yamini's idea original?
qa.a: It linked maths, music and computer science into something none of them could make alone.

qa.q: How might Yamini have felt when Zeenat said rhythm was fractions?
qa.a: Doubtful and amused at first, then intrigued enough to test it.

grounding: Shows a young adult combining maths, music and coding to create an original educational tool.

Professor's note, Nazia, Department of Architecture, March
Sonali (20) submitted her bus-shelter project this week. Instead of a standard steel design, she combined her architecture training with what she learned in an ecology elective: the roof is planted with local grasses to cool the space, and the seats are angled for monsoon runoff. She interviewed commuters and a botanist before designing it. Some details aren't practical yet, but the thinking across fields is original. I've suggested she enter it in the city design competition and offered to mentor her. I've also asked her to present it to the first-years next month.

qa.q: What did Sonali plant on the roof?
qa.a: Local grasses.

qa.q: What might Sonali have felt when her project broke from the standard design?
